Influence moves the world.

DiscoverSubvertWhat moves a person?
CoordinateOrchestrateWho can move the city?
RememberAdaptWhat changes afterwards?

The promise. A single-player real-time tactical game in a bright retrofuturist city. The player studies people and institutions, earns or extracts cooperation, and times those human actions with traffic, robots and public routines.

The production path. Prove the social loop in a top-down 2D city scene before rebuilding its presentation in 3D Unity. AI agents help make the game; authored data and deterministic rules run it, with no live model calls. The Anima Atlas crew remains on paper.

01
Executive summary

The city is the instrument

Progress comes from understanding a person well enough to ask for something they can actually do.

Pillar 1

Subvert people

Discover their work, access, loyalties, ambitions and vulnerabilities. Choose an approach suited to the person.

Pillar 2

Orchestrate the city

Combine people, schedules, vehicles, buildings and robots in a timed causal chain.

Pillar 3

Adapt to consequences

People remember treatment. Influence fades, resentment grows, and institutions learn.

Signature moment. A clerk who once accepted help with a debt later refuses a threat, remembers who applied it, and changes a subsequent operation. The reaction is authored and readable to the player.

Living decision · 24 September 2026: the first playable proof is 2D and top-down. Camera, art, code and engine may change later; the observable clue, bounded request, coordinated consequence and NPC memory must survive that change.

02
Game mechanics

Observe, influence, arrange

A person is a character with capabilities and memory, not a generic converted unit.

Observe→Investigate→Influence→Coordinate→Live with the result

What the player reads

Occupations, routines, access points and relationships surface through the street. Personal leverage must be discovered through a fair clue. The interface shows known facts separately from suspicion.

What the player does

Choose a known lever, an authored approach and a bounded request. Then coordinate willing or reluctant people while movement, guards and machines continue in real time.

First mission · Records Office

2D PoC: one top-down block with the Records Office, café, service lane and tram stop; Harold the clerk, a café worker and a maintenance technician have authored routines and influence responses. One guard tests timing. A single player-directed field operative can retrieve an exposed document; citizens create the opportunity. Other people, a vehicle and a robot begin as scheduled cues. A later Unity slice can expand to 10–15 visible NPCs, two guards and fuller city movement.

1 / Read the block

Watch the café, office entrance, service lane and guard routine.

2 / Find leverage

Observe Harold meeting a collector; follow that clue to confirm the debt.

3 / Arrange the window

Harold can carry the document out; alternatively, the technician opens a service route and the café worker draws the guard away so the operative can retrieve it.

4 / Carry the consequence

Leave with the document. Witnesses, evidence and each person's response become persistent state.

Win: extract the document. Lose: it becomes irretrievable or an explicit, visible exposure threshold is crossed. Local alarms can still have recovery paths. All NPC requests check capability, access, trust, suspicion and remembered treatment.

How missions and areas connect

Mission template

Define an objective, a target, discoverable clues, people with relevant capabilities, at least two viable causal routes, a clear failure threshold, a recovery path and a lasting consequence. The Records Office becomes the first tested instance of this template.

Area template

Define public and restricted zones, entrances, observation points, social hubs, schedule anchors, transit links and security responses. Share named people and their state across areas, so a clerk seen at the café can appear later at the tram stop.

New missions should recombine existing people and actions before adding a new mechanic. A new area earns its place by creating a new decision, not merely more streets. PoC hypothesis: one ordinary field operative makes movement and extraction legible while influenced citizens supply access; playtests should check whether this weakens the game's social focus.

03
AI architecture · build-time studio

One lead, clear owners

A proposed 15-agent Anima Atlas roster. No agent has been registered or dispatched.

Anima reference. Anima preserves each agent's identity and work history across sessions, with live inter-agent messaging so Aster can coordinate handoffs and review.

Lead

Aster · goal tree, GDD, dispatch, review and routine decisions.

Design

Motive · influence and memory rules.

Fable · characters and dialogue.

Waymark · mission, clues and recovery.

Engineering

Keel · portable rules, data, save state.

Latch · 2D PoC, then Unity gameplay.

Pulse · NPC routines, later city simulation.

Splice · import, validation and tools.

Presentation

Vela · Blender 3D environment.

Forma · people, rigs, animation.

Glint · tech art and lighting.

Glyph · UI and accessibility.

Chime · audio.

Quality

Suture · QA and playtests.

Redline · code review and profiling.

What reaches the player: Motive and Fable's reviewed rules make Harold's response personal; Waymark and Suture make both access routes discoverable; Keel, Latch and Pulse make the response consistent in play; the presentation crew makes jobs, routes and consequences readable and audible.

AssessAster picks the next bounded objective.
AssignOne owner receives a contract and evidence target.
ReviewSuture or Redline checks the relevant surface.
ContinueAster accepts or routes a fix, then reports the milestone.

Autonomy: Aster handles routine choices and keeps the user out of day-to-day dispatch. Escalation is for a pillar change, new paid spend, release or publication, destructive action, or unresolved strategic conflict. Model lanes: Opus 5.5 for lead, design, narrative, art briefs and player-facing QA; Sol 6 for engine, Unity, simulation, tools and code review. Exact model identifiers are confirmed at activation.

One agent, one wow. Motive authors Harold's context-sensitive reaction table. Fable writes the response; Keel fixes its schema; Latch and Pulse implement the memory flag and deterministic behavior. Aster accepts the reviewed output. No model runs during play.
04
Technical strategy · course pillars

Prove the loop before 3D

The same game rules can be tested cheaply in 2D, then carried into a richer Unity presentation.

AI development pipelineAster briefs design, engineering and art; owners produce versioned artifacts; reviewers return findings; Aster integrates one canonical GDD.
Technical constraintsAuthored IDs, actions, clues, mission graph and save flags must agree. Splice rejects unknown IDs. Both PoC and Unity slice run offline.
Token budgetOne planning/review pass estimates 71,000 input and 17,800 output tokens, 88,800 total. This is an estimate, not measured usage; coding and image work need separate budgets.

PoC first · engine choice is provisional

Build one playable top-down city scene using generated art for atmosphere and hand-authored walkable areas, interaction points and NPC routes. Phaser is the current browser-first hypothesis for quick playtesting and an HTML deliverable; Godot remains an option if its scene editor becomes more useful than browser iteration. Keep NPC facts, action IDs, mission states and save flags in plain data so the later 3D Unity build can reproduce the same behavior.

PoC passes when: a new player discovers the debt clue, completes the document objective through either Harold or the service route, understands a refusal, and sees one later response changed by remembered treatment. Art quality is judged by city readability and mood; generated pixels never define collision or mission truth.

1 · One blockProve the social loop, two routes and one remembered consequence.
2 · Connected placesAdd tram avenue and repair forecourt; the same people move between scenes.
3 · Small districtCombine retrieval, diversion and exposure missions as institutions adapt.
4 · Unity 3DRebuild camera, spaces and presentation while replaying the same rule and mission cases.

Biggest constraint and response

Cross-agent consistency is the biggest technical constraint because a plausible design handoff can give Harold an action, clue or access right that the mission graph and Unity data do not contain. Keel maintains one ID catalogue and typed output schema; Splice rejects invalid references; Suture tests the full player path; Aster resolves conflicts before any data is imported.

Prompt, API and engine bounds

Each agent receives the relevant GDD slice, approved IDs, task scope, output schema and reviewer; it marks unknown facts rather than inventing them. Motive's Harold rule must cite the collector clue and an allowed archive action; Waymark supplies two viable routes; the art brief keeps visual surfaces separate from walkable geometry. Before activation, Aster measures Opus 5.5 and Sol 6 context limits, request limits and prices, queues calls at review gates, records token use and resumes from saved artifacts after a failed call. Neither playable version has a model dependency.

Planning envelope: design/architecture 27k input + 7.2k output; build planning 16k + 4k; presentation 18k + 4.6k; independent review 10k + 2k. Total 88.8k tokens for one pass. Revisions, coding and image generation are separate; actual usage must be measured.

Open logic gaps: RO-01 tests whether the collector clue is discoverable; RO-02 defines the exposure threshold and recovery rule before either is treated as shippable. RO-03 tests whether the service route is truly independent of Harold.

05
Visual direction · new concept sheet

Tomorrow has foot traffic

The ordinary city must be appealing, busy and easy to read from a tactical camera.

Places with social seams

Records block: civic entrance, café and service lane offer several ways to reach one archive. Tram avenue: conductor, stop and arriving crowds create a timing puzzle. Repair forecourt: technician and robot charger make maintenance access consequential.

Materials, camera and UI

Curved cream buildings, teal enamel, coral transit accents, warm glass and chrome. Workwear silhouettes reveal occupations. Tickets, route maps and clipped dossiers inspire the interface; teal signals knowledge, coral risk and gold opportunity. Test transit, trees and UI for target visibility at tactical zoom.

For the PoC, generate a clean top-down block image and a small set of occupational character visuals in this palette; draw interaction markers and readable paths over it. The image is a visual layer, while walkability, cover and access are authored game data. The held 136 × 136 m Unity sector and 3D clearances come later. The earlier Syndicate-oriented GDD informs this HTML layout, not gameplay direction.

Source basis. Project retrofuture cityfill concept artwork and earlier Suborned design record; conversation decisions for Subvert → Orchestrate → Adapt, the Records Office proof, and the course's AI development pipeline, technical constraints and token budget.
